title: Study of Compounds: Hydrogen Chloride
tagline: One laboratory preparation, the solubility that makes it a fountain, and the reactions that define an acid.

overview.intro: Hydrogen chloride is the first compound the syllabus studies in detail, and it sets the pattern for the other three: preparation, physical properties, chemical properties, then uses and tests. The preparation is a simple displacement reaction in a flask, the standout physical property is its enormous solubility in water, and the chemical properties are those of a strong acid — with metals, oxides, carbonates and ammonia. Learn the acid pattern here and the same reactions recur for nitric and sulphuric acids with only the specifics changed.

facts.label: Preparation
facts.value: Sodium chloride heated with concentrated sulphuric acid in a glass flask.

facts.label: Solubility
facts.value: Highly soluble in water; one volume dissolves about 500 volumes of the gas.

facts.label: Acid behaviour
facts.value: In water it ionises completely, giving hydrogen ions as the only positive ion.

facts.label: Test
facts.value: White fumes with ammonia and a white precipitate with silver nitrate soluble in ammonia.

learningOutcomes: Describe the laboratory preparation of hydrogen chloride, including drying and collection of the gas.
State the physical properties of hydrogen chloride and explain its solubility using the fountain experiment.
Write equations for the reactions of hydrogen chloride with metals, metal oxides, carbonates and ammonia.
Explain why hydrogen chloride does not show acid behaviour until it dissolves in water.
Carry out the tests for hydrogen chloride gas and for chloride ions in solution.

blocks.text: The preparation is a straightforward reaction in which a less volatile acid displaces a more volatile one from its salt. Sodium chloride is mixed with concentrated sulphuric acid in a round-bottomed flask; gentle heating first produces sodium hydrogen sulphate and hydrogen chloride, and stronger heating later completes the reaction. Because hydrogen chloride is heavier than air and does not react with it, the gas is collected in an upright jar by upward displacement of air, with an inverted dry funnel at the mouth of the jar to reduce escape. The gas is dried by passing it through concentrated sulphuric acid, which is the correct choice because it does not react with the acidic gas. All glassware must be dry, since the gas dissolves in any water present and would simply be absorbed.

items: Reagents: common salt and concentrated sulphuric acid, chosen because sulphuric acid is less volatile.
Gentle heating gives NaHSO4 and HCl; stronger heating with excess salt gives Na2SO4 and HCl.
The gas is collected in an upright jar by upward displacement of air because it is denser than air.
Drying uses concentrated sulphuric acid; an inverted funnel over the mouth reduces back-suction.

items.note: NaCl + H2SO4 → NaHSO4 + HCl at just above 200 °C, giving a steady stream of the gas.

items.text: Loss of gas without a funnel
items.note: Rapid dissolution in water draws liquid back up the delivery tube and can crack the flask.

items.meaning: Evaporates readily; hydrochloric acid is more volatile than sulphuric acid, so it is displaced.
Collection of a gas denser than air: the jar stands upright and the lighter air is driven out above the incoming gas.
Rush of water into hot apparatus when a very soluble gas dissolves too quickly.

learn.title: Physical properties and the fountain that proves solubility

blocks.text: Hydrogen chloride is a colourless gas with a pungent, choking smell and it fumes in moist air, because the tiny droplets of hydrochloric acid it forms scatter light. It is heavier than air, which fixes the collection method, and it is extraordinarily soluble in water — one volume of the gas dissolves in roughly five hundred volumes of water. That solubility is demonstrated by the fountain experiment: a dry flask filled with the gas has a little water forced in through a tap, the gas dissolves at once, the pressure inside drops, and water rushes in from a reservoir below as a fine spray. The conclusion students must state is not simply that the gas dissolves, but that the pressure difference created by its rapid dissolution is what drives the fountain.

items: Colourless, pungent gas that fumes in moist air because droplets of hydrochloric acid form.
Denser than air, so it is collected in an upright jar by upward displacement of air.
Very soluble in water, roughly one to five hundred, demonstrated by the fountain experiment.
It liquefies under pressure to give liquid hydrogen chloride, which does not conduct — ions appear only in water.

items.note: A small jet of water enters the gas-filled flask, dissolves the gas and produces a partial vacuum that draws a spray of water upwards.

items.text: Moist air over a jar of the gas
items.note: White mist forms as the gas meets water vapour and makes tiny droplets of acid.

items.meaning: Giving off visible mist because the gas reacts with moisture in the air.
The aqueous solution of hydrogen chloride, a strong acid that ionises completely.
About five hundred volumes of the gas dissolve in one volume of water, which is what drives the fountain experiment.

blocks.text: Dry hydrogen chloride is almost inert: it does not turn litmus, does not attack metals and does not react with carbonates. All the familiar acid behaviour appears only after it dissolves in water, where the molecule ionises completely into hydrogen and chloride ions — the definition of an acid in action. In solution it reacts with metals above hydrogen in the activity series to give the metal chloride and hydrogen; with metal oxides to give salt and water; with carbonates and hydrogencarbonates to give salt, water and carbon dioxide; and with ammonia to give dense white fumes of ammonium chloride. Notice that the four reaction types are exactly the pattern a base or an oxide neutralises, and the salt formed always carries the metal with the same valence it shows in the oxide.

items: Metal + acid → salt + hydrogen, as zinc gives zinc chloride with hydrogen evolved.
Metal oxide + acid → salt + water, which is neutralisation in its oxide form.
Metal carbonate + acid → salt + water + carbon dioxide, the standard test for carbonates.
Ammonia + hydrogen chloride → ammonium chloride, dense white fumes used to identify either gas.

items.note: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl2 + H2, with hydrogen confirmed by the squeaky pop test.
CuO + 2HCl → CuCl2 + H2O, the blue-green solution showing copper(II) chloride.

learn.title: Tests for the gas, tests for chloride, and aqua regia

blocks.text: Three tests complete the study of this compound. For the gas itself, damp blue litmus turns red and the gas fumes in moist air; more specifically, a glass rod dipped in ammonia and brought near gives dense white fumes of ammonium chloride. In solution, the chloride ion is identified with silver nitrate, which gives a white precipitate soluble in aqueous ammonia; the same precipitate appears when concentrated sulphuric acid is added to a chloride and the mixture is warmed, giving hydrogen chloride that fumes in moist air. The fourth idea worth knowing is aqua regia, a mixture of concentrated hydrochloric and nitric acids in the ratio three to one, which dissolves gold and platinum by providing both chloride ions that complex the metal and nitrate that supplies the oxidising power. It is the classic demonstration that a metal too noble for any single acid can still be dissolved.

items: Gas test: fumes in moist air, turns damp blue litmus red, white fumes with ammonia.
Chloride in solution: silver nitrate gives a white precipitate that dissolves in aqueous ammonia.
Concentrated sulphuric acid with a chloride gives hydrogen chloride gas, identified by white fumes with ammonia.
Aqua regia is three parts concentrated hydrochloric acid to one part concentrated nitric acid and dissolves gold.

items.note: Add dilute nitric acid then silver nitrate: a white curdy precipitate appears, which dissolves in aqueous ammonia.
The metal enters solution as a chloro-complex while nitrate provides the oxidation needed to start the reaction.

items.meaning: Mixture of concentrated hydrochloric and nitric acids, three to one, capable of dissolving gold.
Anionic species such as tetrachloroaurate that keep gold in solution.
Silver nitrate gives a white precipitate with chloride that dissolves in ammonia, distinguishing it from sulphate.

learn.title: Uses, hazards and how to answer description questions

blocks.text: Hydrochloric acid earns its place in industry because it is a strong, cheap acid: it removes rust and scale from metals before plating or painting, it is used to make chlorides such as ammonium chloride and to acidify dye baths, and in the stomach it works with pepsin to digest protein. The laboratory hazards follow from the same properties — it is corrosive, it fumes, and it attacks many metals, so it is stored away from them and always handled with a fume draft. For examination answers, describe a preparation in numbered steps with the reason for each choice, and describe a property as observation plus explanation rather than a bare statement. The marking schemes reward the reasoning: why concentrated sulphuric acid for drying, why downward delivery, why an inverted funnel.

items: Uses: pickling of steel, manufacture of chlorides, pH control in dyeing, and digestive acid in the stomach.
Storage: away from metals and in stoppered bottles because the gas escapes and fumes in moist air.
Safety: corrosive to skin and eyes; use a fume draft because the vapour irritates the respiratory tract.
Answer style: numbered steps for preparation, observation plus reason for every property question.

items.note: Dilute hydrochloric acid removes the oxide scale so that the zinc coating can bond to clean metal.
Ammonia and hydrogen chloride combine directly, giving white crystals used in dry batteries and fluxes.

items.meaning: Acid treatment that removes oxide scale from metal surfaces before finishing.
Local exhaust ventilation that draws corrosive vapour away from the operator.
Industrial name for technical grade hydrochloric acid used in cleaning, pickling and food processing.

keyPoints: Hydrochloric acid is made by heating common salt with concentrated sulphuric acid, a less volatile acid displacing a more volatile one.
The gas is dried with concentrated sulphuric acid and collected in an upright jar by upward displacement of air.
Hydrogen chloride is colourless, pungent, denser than air, fumes in moist air and is very soluble in water.
The fountain experiment shows that rapid dissolution lowers the pressure inside the flask.
Dry hydrogen chloride shows no acid behaviour; ions appear only when it dissolves in water.
The acid reacts with metals to give salt and hydrogen, with oxides to give salt and water, with carbonates to give salt, water and carbon dioxide.
Ammonia and hydrogen chloride give dense white fumes of ammonium chloride.
Chloride ions are confirmed by silver nitrate giving a white precipitate soluble in aqueous ammonia.
Aqua regia, three parts hydrochloric acid to one part nitric acid, dissolves gold.
Main uses: pickling of metals, manufacture of chlorides and pH control in dyeing.
examFocus: Preparation answers need reagents, apparatus arrangement, drying agent, collection method and one reason for each choice.
Explain the fountain in terms of pressure, not solubility alone: the pressure drop is what the marker wants.
Contrast dry gas with aqueous acid whenever acid behaviour is asked; the ionisation point is the heart of the answer.
The chloride test is a three-part answer: acidify, add silver nitrate, then show solubility in ammonia.

vocabulary.meaning: Evaporates readily at comparatively low temperature.
Method of collecting a gas denser than air in an upright jar, with the air driven out at the top.
Drawback of water into apparatus caused by very rapid gas dissolution.
Giving off visible mist of droplets when the gas meets moist air.
Three-to-one mixture of concentrated hydrochloric and nitric acids that dissolves gold.
Acid cleaning of metal surfaces to remove oxide scale.
Formation of ions when hydrogen chloride dissolves in water.
Reaction of an acid with a base or oxide to give salt and water.

questions.prompt: Hydrogen chloride gas is collected by:
options: Upward displacement of air in an upright jar
Downward displacement of air in an inverted jar
questions.answer: Upward displacement of air in an upright jar
questions.explanation: The gas is denser than air and very soluble in water, so it displaces the lighter air upward in a jar held upright.

questions.prompt: The drying agent used for hydrogen chloride gas is:
questions.explanation: The gas is acidic, so an alkaline or water-reactive drying agent is unsuitable; concentrated sulphuric acid is neutral to it.

questions.prompt: Dry hydrogen chloride fails to turn litmus blue then red because:
options: It produces no hydrogen ions until it dissolves in water
questions.answer: It produces no hydrogen ions until it dissolves in water
questions.explanation: Acid behaviour depends on hydrogen ions, which appear only when the molecule ionises in water.

questions.prompt: Aqua regia dissolves gold because it:
options: Provides chloride ions for complex formation and nitrate as oxidant
Reduces gold to a lower oxide
questions.answer: Provides chloride ions for complex formation and nitrate as oxidant
questions.explanation: Chloride ions combine with gold while nitrate oxidises it, and neither component alone can do the job.

questions.prompt: Hydrogen chloride fumes in moist air because it dissolves in the moisture to form tiny droplets of __________ acid.
questions.explanation: The visible mist is hydrochloric acid droplets suspended in the air.

questions.prompt: The mixture of concentrated hydrochloric and nitric acids used to dissolve gold is called aqua __________.
questions.explanation: Aqua regia is three parts hydrochloric acid to one part nitric acid and attacks metals no single acid can touch.

questions.prompt: Write the equation for the laboratory preparation of hydrogen chloride from sodium chloride and concentrated sulphuric acid, and state the condition.
questions.answer: NaCl + H2SO4 → NaHSO4 + HCl, carried out with gentle heating; if excess sodium chloride is heated strongly the second stage gives Na2SO4 + 2HCl instead.
questions.explanation: Sulphuric acid being less volatile displaces the more volatile hydrogen chloride from its salt.

questions.prompt: Describe the test for hydrogen chloride gas.
questions.answer: Bring a glass rod dipped in concentrated ammonia near the gas: dense white fumes of ammonium chloride form. Alternatively the gas turns moist blue litmus red and gives fumes in moist air.
questions.explanation: Ammonia is the specific test because the product is a solid visible as white smoke.

questions.prompt: Give one use each of hydrogen chloride and hydrochloric acid.
questions.answer: Hydrochloric acid is used to remove rust and scale from metals before galvanising, and hydrogen chloride is used to make ammonium chloride and other chloride salts.
questions.explanation: Both uses follow from the same property: a strong acid that forms soluble chloride salts.

questions.prompt: Explain, with reference to ions, why hydrogen chloride gas is not acidic but its aqueous solution is.
questions.answer: In the gaseous state hydrogen chloride consists of discrete covalent molecules in which electrons are shared between hydrogen and chlorine, so there are no charged particles and no acid behaviour — dry gas does not change the colour of litmus paper. When the gas dissolves in water, the highly polar bond breaks heterolytically and the hydrogen ion transfers to a water molecule, forming hydronium ions and leaving chloride ions in solution. It is these free hydrogen ions that give the characteristic acid reactions with indicators, metals, oxides and carbonates. The molecule itself is never acidic; the ions produced in water are.
questions.explanation: Acidity is a property of hydrogen ions in solution, and those ions exist only after ionisation in water.

questions.prompt: Describe how chloride ions in solution are identified, and explain why bromide and iodide behave differently with the same reagent.
questions.answer: Acidify the solution with dilute nitric acid to remove interfering ions, then add silver nitrate solution. Chloride gives a white precipitate of silver chloride which dissolves readily in aqueous ammonia. Bromide would give a pale yellow precipitate only sparingly soluble in ammonia, and iodide a yellow precipitate insoluble in ammonia but soluble in potassium iodide. The difference follows from lattice energy: as the halide ion grows from chloride to iodide the silver halide lattice becomes less soluble in ammonia because the larger ions form weaker complexes under these conditions, so solubility behaviour distinguishes the three.
questions.explanation: Precipitate colour plus solubility in ammonia is the pair of observations that separates the halide ions.

questions.prompt: A colourless gas turns damp blue litmus red, gives dense white fumes with ammonia, and its solution gives a white precipitate with silver nitrate that dissolves in ammonia. Identify the gas and the ion in solution, and explain why the gas cannot be collected over water.
questions.answer: The gas is hydrogen chloride and the ion in solution is the chloride ion. Turning damp litmus red shows an acidic gas, white fumes with ammonia identify hydrogen chloride as ammonium chloride forms, and the silver nitrate result with solubility in ammonia is the specific test for chloride. The gas cannot be collected over water because it is extraordinarily soluble — roughly five hundred volumes dissolve in one volume of water — so it would dissolve rather than displace the water; an upright jar with upward displacement of air is used instead, taking advantage of its greater density than air.
questions.explanation: Three independent signs converge on hydrogen chloride, and its solubility rules out water displacement collection.
